query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) interlayer can serve as an effective intermediate material between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr in fusion reactor components by mitigating thermal expansion mismatch and enhancing radiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy as synthesized with refined grain structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin RHEA interlayer between the W plasma-facing component and the CuCrZr heat sink.
generation.conditions: Operating under extreme thermal loads, high neutron irradiation, and cyclic thermal stresses typical of fusion reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent interfaces enabled by the refined nanocrystalline morphology and tailored interphase chemistry.
generation.mechanism: The RHEA interlayer is expected to reduce interfacial stress through improved thermal expansion matching and to retard defect formation under irradiation by leveraging its enhanced thermal stability and radiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved interfacial bonding, reduced thermal stresses, and enhanced durability of the W/CuCrZr joint compared with a direct bond.
generation.baseline: A direct joint between tungsten and CuCrZr without an interlayer, which is prone to high thermal mismatch stress and radiation-induced degradation.
generation.boundary: The precise alloy composition, optimal thickness of the interlayer, and its long-term behavior under full fusion reactor conditions remain to be quantified.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative extent of stress mitigation and radiation resistance improvement, necessitating further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate multilayer samples consisting of a tungsten layer, a RHEA interlayer of controlled thickness, and a CuCrZr layer. Subject these samples to accelerated thermal cycling and neutron/ion irradiation to mimic fusion reactor conditions. Include control samples without the interlayer for comparison.
measurements: Interfacial shear strength and bonding integrity via mechanical testing
Residual stress analysis at the interfaces using X-ray diffraction or Raman spectroscopy
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to monitor defect evolution and grain structure
Assessment of thermal conductivity and expansion mismatch via in situ experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the RHEA interlayer show no statistically significant improvement in interfacial bonding, residual stress reduction, or defect mitigation compared to the direct W/CuCrZr samples, or if the interlayer degrades under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] .
